claim: COX6B2 is expressed in human lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) tumors.
source: We describe human COX6B2, a component of cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV). COX6B2 is expressed in human lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and expression correlates with reduced survival time.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1E-F showing COX6B2 protein in LUAD tumors and cell lines, and IHC data in Figure 1G showing COX6B2 staining in LUAD tissues.

claim: Elevated COX6B2 expression correlates with reduced survival time in LUAD patients.
source: COX6B2 is expressed in human lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and expression correlates with reduced survival time.
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating significant correlation between high COX6B2 expression and poor overall survival (p=1.6×10−4) and time to first progression (p=9.4×10−5) in LUAD patients.

claim: COX6B2 enhances activity of complex IV.
source: COX6B2, but not its somatic isoform COX6B1, enhances activity of complex IV, increasing oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and NAD+ generation.
evidence: Supported by direct complex IV activity measurements in Figure 3B showing ~25% increase in complex IV activity in COX6B2-V5 overexpressing cells.

claim: COX6B2 increases oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS).
source: COX6B2, but not its somatic isoform COX6B1, enhances activity of complex IV, increasing oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and NAD+ generation.
evidence: Supported by oxygen consumption rate measurements in Figure 2D and 2F showing significant enhancement in basal, ATP-linked, maximal and reserve OCR in COX6B2-V5 expressing cells.

claim: COX6B2 increases NAD+ generation.
source: COX6B2, but not its somatic isoform COX6B1, enhances activity of complex IV, increasing oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and NAD+ generation.
evidence: Supported by NAD+/NADH ratio measurements in Figure 2H showing elevated NAD+/NADH in COX6B2-V5 cells.

claim: COX6B2-expressing cancer cells display a proliferative advantage, particularly in low oxygen.
source: Consequently, COX6B2-expressing cancer cells display a proliferative advantage, particularly in low oxygen.
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data in Figure 4A showing increased DNA synthesis, and hypoxia experiments in Figure 4D showing COX6B2-V5 cells maintain higher proliferation rates under low oxygen conditions.

claim: Depletion of COX6B2 attenuates OXPHOS.
source: Conversely, depletion of COX6B2 attenuates OXPHOS and collapses mitochondrial membrane potential leading to cell death or senescence.
evidence: Supported by OCR measurements in Figure 5A-B showing decreased basal, ATP-linked, maximal and reserve OCR following COX6B2 depletion.

claim: Depletion of COX6B2 collapses mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Conversely, depletion of COX6B2 attenuates OXPHOS and collapses mitochondrial membrane potential leading to cell death or senescence.
evidence: Supported by JC-1 staining data in Figure 5E showing decreased mitochondrial membrane potential following COX6B2 depletion.

claim: Depletion of COX6B2 leads to cell death or senescence.
source: Conversely, depletion of COX6B2 attenuates OXPHOS and collapses mitochondrial membrane potential leading to cell death or senescence.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6 showing increased cleaved caspase-3 and PARP (markers of apoptosis) and increased β-galactosidase staining (marker of senescence) following COX6B2 depletion.

claim: COX6B2 is necessary for growth of human tumor xenografts in mice.
source: COX6B2 is both necessary and sufficient for growth of human tumor xenografts in mice.
evidence: Supported by xenograft data in Figure 7C-D showing that depletion of COX6B2 severely reduces tumor growth and final tumor mass.

claim: COX6B2 is sufficient for growth of human tumor xenografts in mice.
source: COX6B2 is both necessary and sufficient for growth of human tumor xenografts in mice.
evidence: Supported by xenograft data in Figure 7A-B showing enhanced growth of COX6B2-V5 expressing cells in vivo with 4X greater tumor mass than control after 38 days.

claim: COX6B1 does not enhance activity of complex IV.
source: COX6B2, but not its somatic isoform COX6B1, enhances activity of complex IV, increasing oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) and NAD+ generation.
evidence: Supported by complex IV activity measurements in Figure 3C showing minimal, statistically insignificant increase in activity following COX6B1-V5 overexpression.

claim: COX6B2 is a testis-specific subunit of cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV).
source: Similarly, COX6B2 is a testis-specific subunit of cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) (Hüttemann et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hüttemann et al., 2003.

claim: mRNA encoding COX6B2 is undetectable in normal tissue.
source: mRNA encoding of either LDHC or COX6B2 is undetectable in normal tissue, but both are upregulated in a number of different tumor derived cell lines, classifying them as CTAs (Maxfield et al., 2015, (CTpedia (http://www.cta.lncc.br/index.php))).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maxfield et al., 2015 and CTpedia database.

claim: COX6B2 is upregulated in tumor derived cell lines.
source: mRNA encoding of either LDHC or COX6B2 is undetectable in normal tissue, but both are upregulated in a number of different tumor derived cell lines, classifying them as CTAs (Maxfield et al., 2015, (CTpedia (http://www.cta.lncc.br/index.php))).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maxfield et al., 2015 and CTpedia database, and by immunoblot data in Figure 1F showing COX6B2 protein in LUAD cell lines.

claim: COX6B2 is classified as a cancer testis antigen (CTA).
source: mRNA encoding of either LDHC or COX6B2 is undetectable in normal tissue, but both are upregulated in a number of different tumor derived cell lines, classifying them as CTAs (Maxfield et al., 2015, (CTpedia (http://www.cta.lncc.br/index.php))).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maxfield et al., 2015 and CTpedia database, and by the expression pattern shown in Figure 1 (expressed in testis and tumors but not normal tissues).

claim: COX6B2 is essential for survival of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines.
source: In a large-scale lossof-function analysis to annotate the contribution of individual CTAs to neoplastic behaviors, we found that COX6B2 is essential for survival of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines (Maxfield et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maxfield et al., 2015 and by data in Figure 6 showing that COX6B2 depletion leads to cell death and senescence.

claim: COX6B2 is a nuclear encoded, sperm-specific component of complex IV.
source: COX6B2 is a nuclear encoded, sperm-specific component of complex IV (Hüttemann et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hüttemann et al., 2003.

claim: Complex IV is the rate-limiting step for ATP production by the electron transport chain (ETC).
source: By transferring electrons from reduced cytochrome c to O2, complex IV is the rate-limiting step for ATP production by the electron transport chain (ETC).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the electron transport chain.

claim: Thirteen subunits make up complex IV: three are mitochondrial encoded and ten are derived from nuclear DNA.
source: Thirteen subunits make up complex IV: three are mitochondrial encoded and ten are derived from nuclear DNA.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about complex IV structure.

claim: Six of the 10 nuclear encoded subunits of complex IV have tissue-specific isoforms.
source: Six of the 10 nuclear encoded subunits have tissue-specific isoforms that permit regulation of this complex in response to environmental cues (e.g. pH, hormones, metals, ATP/ADP ratio etc.) (Kadenbach and Hüttemann, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kadenbach and Hüttemann, 2015.

claim: The somatic isoform of COX6B2 is COX6B1.
source: The somatic isoform of COX6B2 is COX6B1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the COX6B protein family.

claim: COX6B2 and COX6B1 share 58% amino acid identity and ~80% similarity.
source: These two proteins share 58% amino acid identity and ~80% similarity.
evidence: This is a factual statement about protein sequence comparison.

claim: COX6B1/2 are the only complex IV subunits that are not membrane bound.
source: Based on structural information, it is apparent that COX6B1/2 are the only complex IV subunits that are not membrane bound.
evidence: Based on inference from structural information of complex IV.

claim: COX6B1/B2 localization is confined to the intermembrane space where cytochrome c associates.
source: Instead, their localization is confined to the intermembrane space where cytochrome c associates.
evidence: Based on structural information and inference about protein localization.

claim: COX6B1/B2 participate in dimerization of complex IV and cytochrome c association.
source: It is inferred that COX6B1/B2 participate in dimerization of complex IV and cytochrome c association (Sampson and Alleyne, 2001; Tsukihara et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sampson and Alleyne, 2001 and Tsukihara et al., 1996, and explicitly stated as an inference.

claim: COX6B1 is essential for complex IV activity.
source: While limited, studies on COX6B1 indicate that it is essential for complex IV activity.
evidence: Based on inference from studies showing that mutations in COX6B1 abrogate complex IV assembly.

claim: Human mutations in COX6B1 (R20C or R20H) abrogate complex IV assembly and lead to severe cardiac defects.
source: In particular, human mutations in COX6B1 (R20C or R20H) abrogate complex IV assembly and lead to severe cardiac defects (Abdulhag et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abdulhag et al., 2015.

claim: Removal of COX6B1 from assembled complexes enhances complex IV activity.
source: In addition, biochemical analysis indicates that removal of COX6B1 from assembled complexes enhances complex IV activity, implying a negative regulatory role for COX6B1 (Weishaupt and Kadenbach, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weishaupt and Kadenbach, 1992.

claim: COX6B1 has a negative regulatory role in complex IV activity.
source: In addition, biochemical analysis indicates that removal of COX6B1 from assembled complexes enhances complex IV activity, implying a negative regulatory role for COX6B1 (Weishaupt and Kadenbach, 1992).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that removal of COX6B1 enhances complex IV activity, as cited from Weishaupt and Kadenbach, 1992.

claim: There are no reports detailing the function of COX6B2.
source: To-date no reports detail the function of COX6B2 nor indicate the physiological relevance of this sperm-specific subunit to fertility.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of writing.

claim: There are no reports indicating the physiological relevance of COX6B2 to fertility.
source: To-date no reports detail the function of COX6B2 nor indicate the physiological relevance of this sperm-specific subunit to fertility.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of writing.

claim: There are no reports describing mechanism(s) that regulate COX6B1 or COX6B2 expression.
source: Furthermore, there are no reports describing mechanism(s) that regulate COX6B1 or COX6B2 expression.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature at the time of writing.

claim: Elevated COX6B2 expression is associated with significantly shorter overall survival time in NSCLC patients.
source: Strikingly, elevated expression of COX6B2 is associated with significantly shorter overall survival (OS) time (p=5.3×10−6, log rank test; hazard ratio (HR): 1.46; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.24–1.73) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: COX6B2 expression positively correlates with time to first progression in NSCLC patients.
source: In addition, COX6B2 expression positively correlates with time to first progression (FP) (p=4.1×10−4, log rank test; HR: 1.63; 95% CI: 1.24–2.14) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There is a strong correlation between COX6B2 expression and overall survival in LUAD.
source: Separation of the two major histological subtypes of NSCLC revealed a strong correlation for both outcomes in LUAD (OS: p=1.6×10−4, log rank test; HR: 1.59; 95% CI: 1.25–2.03; FP: p=9.4×10−5, log rank test; HR: 1.91; 95% CI: 1.37–2.65) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There is a strong correlation between COX6B2 expression and time to first progression in LUAD.
source: Separation of the two major histological subtypes of NSCLC revealed a strong correlation for both outcomes in LUAD (OS: p=1.6×10−4, log rank test; HR: 1.59; 95% CI: 1.25–2.03; FP: p=9.4×10−5, log rank test; HR: 1.91; 95% CI: 1.37–2.65) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The correlation between COX6B2 expression and survival outcomes is not observed in lung squamous carcinoma (LUSC).
source: However, this correlation is not observed in lung squamous carcinoma (LUSC) (OS: p=0.75, log rank test; HR: 1.05; 95% CI: 0.77–1.44; FP: p=0.96, log rank test; HR: 0.99; 95% CI: 0.59–1.65) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis data shown in Figure 1C showing no significant correlation.

claim: COX6B2 mRNA is significantly upregulated in LUAD tumors compared to normal tissues.
source: Analysis of TCGA data sets also revealed a significant upregulation of COX6B2 mRNA in LUAD tumors as compared to normal tissues (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by TCGA RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: COX6B2 protein expression is low or undetectable in normal lung tissue.
source: We found that COX6B2 protein expression is low or undetectable in normal lung tissue, but present in all tumor-derived tissues irrespective of stage and grade (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1E showing minimal COX6B2 in normal lung tissue.

claim: COX6B2 protein is present in all LUAD tumor-derived tissues irrespective of stage and grade.
source: We found that COX6B2 protein expression is low or undetectable in normal lung tissue, but present in all tumor-derived tissues irrespective of stage and grade (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1E and clinical data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: COX6B2 is expressed in LUAD-derived cell lines.
source: A similar pattern is also observed in LUAD-derived cell lines (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1F showing COX6B2 protein in multiple LUAD cell lines.

claim: COX6B2 accumulates in LUAD tumor tissues but not non-malignant tissues.
source: Furthermore, immunohistochemical staining of COX6B2 in a panel of human non-malignant (n = 22) and LUAD tissues (n = 32) indicated accumulation of COX6B2 in tumor, but not non-malignant tissues (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by IHC staining data in Figure 1G showing differential staining between non-malignant and LUAD tissues.

claim: COX6B2 expression in tumors does not have an apparent correlation with the presence or absence of COX6B1.
source: This expression of COX6B2 in tumors does not have an apparent correlation with the presence or absence of COX6B1, the somatic isoform of COX6B2.
evidence: Based on observation of immunoblot data in Figure 1E showing both proteins can be present independently.

claim: COX6B2 accumulation shows a moderate correlation with COXIV, suggesting COX6B2 accumulation coincides with increased mitochondria in cancer cells.
source: We did observe a moderate correlation with the complex IV subunit, COXIV, suggesting COX6B2 accumulation coincides with increased mitochondria in cancer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by Pearson's correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Depletion or overexpression of either COX6B1 or COX6B2 does not impact protein accumulation of the corresponding isoform.
source: Furthermore, depletion or overexpression of either COX6B1 or COX6B2 does not impact protein accumulation of the corresponding isoform (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing independent regulation of the two isoforms.

claim: The regulation of COX6B1 and COX6B2 may be through independent mechanisms.
source: These findings indicate that while the isoforms are closely related in sequence their regulation may be through independent mechanisms.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that depletion or overexpression of one isoform does not affect the other.

claim: Endogenous COX6B2 localizes to the mitochondria in intact LUAD cells.
source: Immunofluorescence of endogenous COX6B2 in intact LUAD cells revealed specific localization to the mitochondria as judged by overlap with Tom20, a mitochondrial resident protein (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1H showing colocalization of COX6B2 with Tom20.

claim: COX6B2 is frequently expressed in LUAD.
source: Thus, COX6B2 is frequently expressed in LUAD, correlates with poor survival and when ectopically expressed can localize to its native mitochondrial location.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of evidence including immunoblots (Figure 1E-F) and IHC (Figure 1G) showing COX6B2 in LUAD samples.

claim: COX6B2 correlates with poor survival in LUAD.
source: Thus, COX6B2 is frequently expressed in LUAD, correlates with poor survival and when ectopically expressed can localize to its native mitochondrial location.
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis in Figure 1B.

claim: When ectopically expressed, COX6B2 can localize to its native mitochondrial location.
source: Thus, COX6B2 is frequently expressed in LUAD, correlates with poor survival and when ectopically expressed can localize to its native mitochondrial location.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1H showing mitochondrial localization of COX6B2.

claim: COX6B2-V5 overexpression is not associated with an increase in mitochondrial DNA.
source: This overexpression is not associated with an increase in mitochondrial DNA or total mitochondria (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial DNA content measurements in Figure 2B.

claim: COX6B2-V5 overexpression is not associated with an increase in total mitochondria.
source: This overexpression is not associated with an increase in mitochondrial DNA or total mitochondria (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: Supported by MitoTracker green staining and flow cytometry analysis in Figure 2C.

claim: COX6B2-V5 expression results in significant enhancement in basal OCR.
source: This analysis revealed a significant enhancement in basal, ATP-linked, maximal and reserve OCR in COX6B2-V5 expressing cells as compared to control (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR measurements in Figure 2D.

claim: COX6B2-V5 expression results in significant enhancement in ATP-linked OCR.
source: This analysis revealed a significant enhancement in basal, ATP-linked, maximal and reserve OCR in COX6B2-V5 expressing cells as compared to control (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR measurements in Figure 2D.

claim: COX6B2-V5 expression results in significant enhancement in maximal OCR.
source: This analysis revealed a significant enhancement in basal, ATP-linked, maximal and reserve OCR in COX6B2-V5 expressing cells as compared to control (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR measurements in Figure 2D.

claim: COX6B2-V5 expression results in significant enhancement in reserve OCR.
source: This analysis revealed a significant enhancement in basal, ATP-linked, maximal and reserve OCR in COX6B2-V5 expressing cells as compared to control (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR measurements in Figure 2D.

claim: A similar trend in OCR enhancement is observed in H2122 cells expressing COX6B2-V5.
source: A similar trend is observed in an independent LUAD cell line, H2122, expressing COX6B2-V5 (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR measurements in Figure 2F for H2122 cells.

claim: The OCR increase in COX6B2-V5 cells is associated with an elevation in total ATP.
source: The OCR increase is associated with an elevation in total ATP in both cell lines (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by ATP content measurements in Figure 2G.

claim: COX6B2-V5 cells show elevated NAD+/NADH ratio.
source: In addition, we observed elevated NAD+/NADH in COX6B2-V5 cells, indicative of an overall increase in electron transport activity (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by NAD+/NADH measurements in Figure 2H.

claim: Elevated NAD+/NADH in COX6B2-V5 cells is indicative of an overall increase in electron transport activity.
source: In addition, we observed elevated NAD+/NADH in COX6B2-V5 cells, indicative of an overall increase in electron transport activity (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known relationship between NAD+/NADH ratio and electron transport activity.

claim: No significant or reproducible alteration in extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) was observed in COX6B2-V5 cells.
source: We did not observe a significant or reproducible alteration in extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) in either setting (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by ECAR measurements in Figure 2I showing no significant difference.

claim: COX6B1-V5 expression has no effect or slightly decreases OCR.
source: COX6B1-V5 expression appears to have no effect or slightly decreases OCR for each parameter (Figure 2K), consistent with prior biochemical studies where COX6B1 removal enhances the activity of complex IV (Weishaupt and Kadenbach, 1992).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR measurements in Figure 2K and citation to Weishaupt and Kadenbach, 1992.

claim: COX6B2-V5 overexpression confers a significant increase (~25%) in complex IV activity in LUAD cell lines.
source: Here, we find that COX6B2-V5 overexpression confers a significant increase (~25%) in complex IV activity in both LUAD cell lines tested (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by direct complex IV activity measurements in Figure 3B.

claim: COX6B1-V5 overexpression results in a minimal, statistically insignificant increase in complex IV activity.
source: In contrast, a minimal, statistically insignificant increase in activity was observed following COX6B1-V5 overexpression (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by complex IV activity measurements in Figure 3C.

claim: The increase in complex IV activity by COX6B2 does not correlate with any apparent increase in the abundance of complex IV.
source: The increase in complex IV activity did not correlate with any apparent increase in the abundance of complex IV as judged by COXIV accumulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by COXIV immunofluorescence quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing no significant difference.

claim: COX6B2 is a rate-limiting subunit of complex IV.
source: This finding suggests that COX6B2 is a rate-limiting subunit of complex IV.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that COX6B2 overexpression increases complex IV activity without increasing complex IV abundance.

claim: >90% of endogenous COX6B2 is found in complex IV dimers or incorporated into supercomplexes.
source: Here, we observed that >90% of endogenous COX6B2 is found in in complex IV dimers or incorporated into supercomplexes.
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE analysis in Figure 3D-E.

claim: >98% of COX6B1 is found in monomeric complex IV.
source: In contrast,>98% COX6B1 is found in monomeric complex IV (Figure 3D–E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE analysis in Figure 3D-E.

claim: >85% of overexpressed COX6B2 is in complex IV dimers/supercomplexes.
source: This trend is maintained when either isoform is overexpressed (>85% of COX6B2 is in complex IV in dimers/supercomplexes versus 40% for COX6B1) (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE analysis in Figure 3F.

claim: 40% of overexpressed COX6B1 is in complex IV dimers/supercomplexes.
source: This trend is maintained when either isoform is overexpressed (>85% of COX6B2 is in complex IV in dimers/supercomplexes versus 40% for COX6B1) (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE analysis in Figure 3F.

claim: Expression of COX6B2-V5, but not COX6B1-V5, shifts the distribution of complex IV from monomers to increased formation of supercomplexes.
source: Here, we found that upon expression of COX6B2-V5, but not COX6B1-V5, the distribution of complex IV shifted from monomers to increased formation of supercomplexes (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE analysis of COXIV distribution in Figure 3G.

claim: COX6B2 overexpressing cells do not display a concomitant induction of superoxide.
source: Indeed, COX6B2 overexpressing cells do not display a concomitant induction of superoxide (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by MitoSOX Red measurements in Figure 3H showing no significant increase in superoxide.

claim: COX6B2 preferentially integrates into dimeric complex IV and supercomplexes.
source: These data indicate that COX6B2 preferentially integrates into dimeric complex IV and supercomplexes, and COX6B2 expression promotes incorporation of complex IV into supercomplexes.
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE analysis in Figure 3D-F showing differential distribution of COX6B2 versus COX6B1.

claim: COX6B2 expression promotes incorporation of complex IV into supercomplexes.
source: These data indicate that COX6B2 preferentially integrates into dimeric complex IV and supercomplexes, and COX6B2 expression promotes incorporation of complex IV into supercomplexes.
evidence: Supported by BN-PAGE analysis in Figure 3G showing increased supercomplex formation upon COX6B2-V5 expression.

claim: Alterations in complex IV distribution by COX6B2 are proposed to enhance mitochondrial OXPHOS while limiting oxidative stress.
source: These alterations in distribution are proposed to enhance mitochondrial OXPHOS while limiting oxidative stress.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed increase in OXPHOS (Figure 2) and lack of increase in ROS (Figure 3H).

claim: COX6B2-V5 overexpression increases DNA synthesis by 50.39 ± 6.35% in HCC515 cells.
source: We observed an increase in DNA synthesis as measured by EdU incorporation of 50.39 ± 6.35% in HCC515 and 38.7 ± 8.4% in H2122 (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data in Figure 4A.

claim: COX6B2-V5 overexpression increases DNA synthesis by 38.7 ± 8.4% in H2122 cells.
source: We observed an increase in DNA synthesis as measured by EdU incorporation of 50.39 ± 6.35% in HCC515 and 38.7 ± 8.4% in H2122 (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data in Figure 4A.

claim: COX6B1-V5 overexpression does not increase DNA synthesis.
source: Notably, an increase is not observed for COX6B1-V5 overexpression consistent with no significant change in OCR (Figure 4A, middle panel; Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data in Figure 4A middle panel showing no significant difference.

claim: COX6B2-V5 overexpression enhances population double rate by 37.16 ± 10.71% in HCC515 cells.
source: In addition, we observed an enhanced population double rate of 37.16 ± 10.71% and 29.88 ± 6.74% for the HCC515 and H2122 cells, respectively (Figure 4B (-) Pyruvate column; compare red and blue bars; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by population doubling rate measurements in Figure 4B.

claim: COX6B2-V5 overexpression enhances population double rate by 29.88 ± 6.74% in H2122 cells.
source: In addition, we observed an enhanced population double rate of 37.16 ± 10.71% and 29.88 ± 6.74% for the HCC515 and H2122 cells, respectively (Figure 4B (-) Pyruvate column; compare red and blue bars; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by population doubling rate measurements in Figure 4B.

claim: Supplementation with pyruvate largely diminishes the proliferative effects of COX6B2-V5 overexpression.
source: Consistent with this model, supplementation with pyruvate, an electron acceptor which drives NAD+ production, largely diminishes the proliferative effects of COX6B2-V5 overexpression (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by population doubling rate measurements with pyruvate supplementation in Figure 4B.

claim: COX6B2-V5 promotes anchorage-independent growth.
source: A similar proliferative advantage is also observed when COX6B2-V5 cells are grown in the absence of extracellular matrix, suggesting that COX6B2 promotes anchorage-independent growth (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by soft agar assay data in Figure 4C showing increased colony formation.

claim: Under low oxygen conditions, control cells reduce EdU incorporation by ~60%.
source: Under these conditions, control cells reduce EdU incorporation by ~60%, while COX6B2-V5 expressing cells decrease incorporation by 15% (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation measurements under hypoxia in Figure 4D.

claim: Under low oxygen conditions, COX6B2-V5 expressing cells decrease EdU incorporation by 15%.
source: Under these conditions, control cells reduce EdU incorporation by ~60%, while COX6B2-V5 expressing cells decrease incorporation by 15% (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation measurements under hypoxia in Figure 4D.

claim: COX6B2 expression can enhance proliferation in both normoxia and low oxygen conditions.
source: This data indicates that COX6B2 expression can enhance proliferation in both normoxia and low oxygen conditions.
evidence: Inferred from EdU incorporation data under normoxia (Figure 4A) and hypoxia (Figure 4D).

claim: HIF-1 is bound near the COX6B2 promoter in human breast cancer cells.
source: ChIP data from human breast cancer cells indicates that HIF-1 is bound near the COX6B2 promoter (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015 and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There are 11 putative HREs (A/G-CGTG) enriched at the HIF-1 peaks near COX6B2.
source: In addition, we also identified 11 putative HREs (A/G-CGTG) which are enriched at the HIF-1 peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: COX6B2 mRNA increases greater than twofold following 12 hr of 2.5% oxygen.
source: Indeed, we observed a greater than twofold increase in COX6B2 but not COX6B1 mRNA following 12 hr of 2.5% oxygen (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4E showing increased COX6B2 mRNA under hypoxia.

claim: COX6B1 mRNA does not increase following 12 hr of 2.5% oxygen.
source: Indeed, we observed a greater than twofold increase in COX6B2 but not COX6B1 mRNA following 12 hr of 2.5% oxygen (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4E showing no significant change in COX6B1 mRNA under hypoxia.

claim: The accumulation of COX6B2 mRNA under hypoxia is associated with stabilization of COX6B2 protein.
source: This accumulation of mRNA was associated with stabilization of COX6B2 protein (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4F showing increased COX6B2 protein under hypoxia.

claim: Under both normoxic or hypoxic conditions, there is no significant alteration in COX6B2 or COX6B1 accumulation when the alternative isoform is overexpressed.
source: Under both normoxic or hypoxic conditions, we did not observe any significant alteration in COX6B2 or COX6B1 accumulation when the alternative isoform was overexpressed, indicating that the changes in expression are not an isoform switch (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The changes in COX6B2 expression under hypoxia are not an isoform switch.
source: Under both normoxic or hypoxic conditions, we did not observe any significant alteration in COX6B2 or COX6B1 accumulation when the alternative isoform was overexpressed, indicating that the changes in expression are not an isoform switch (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that overexpression of one isoform does not affect the other under normoxia or hypoxia.

claim: Enhanced electron transport activity in COX6B2 expressing cells confers a selective advantage by promoting unrestrained proliferation.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that the enhanced electron transport activity in COX6B2 expressing cells confers a selective advantage by promoting key tumorigenic behaviors including unrestrained proliferation, anchorage independent growth and enhanced survival in hypoxia.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on multiple experimental observations including EdU incorporation (Figure 4A), soft agar assays (Figure 4C), and hypoxia experiments (Figure 4D).

claim: Enhanced electron transport activity in COX6B2 expressing cells confers a selective advantage by promoting anchorage independent growth.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that the enhanced electron transport activity in COX6B2 expressing cells confers a selective advantage by promoting key tumorigenic behaviors including unrestrained proliferation, anchorage independent growth and enhanced survival in hypoxia.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on soft agar assay data in Figure 4C.

claim: Enhanced electron transport activity in COX6B2 expressing cells confers a selective advantage by promoting enhanced survival in hypoxia.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that the enhanced electron transport activity in COX6B2 expressing cells confers a selective advantage by promoting key tumorigenic behaviors including unrestrained proliferation, anchorage independent growth and enhanced survival in hypoxia.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on hypoxia proliferation data in Figure 4D.

claim: Reduction of COX6B2 protein using shRNA pools leads to a decrease in basal OCR in HCC515 and H2122 cell lines.
source: Reduction of COX6B2 protein using shRNA pools (four independent sequences) or siRNA pools (two independent sequences), led to a decrease in basal, ATP-linked, maximal and reserve OCR in HCC515 and H2122 cell lines (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR measurements in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Reduction of COX6B2 protein using shRNA pools leads to a decrease in ATP-linked OCR in HCC515 and H2122 cell lines.
source: Reduction of COX6B2 protein using shRNA pools (four independent sequences) or siRNA pools (two independent sequences), led to a decrease in basal, ATP-linked, maximal and reserve OCR in HCC515 and H2122 cell lines (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR measurements in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Reduction of COX6B2 protein using shRNA pools leads to a decrease in maximal OCR in HCC515 and H2122 cell lines.
source: Reduction of COX6B2 protein using shRNA pools (four independent sequences) or siRNA pools (two independent sequences), led to a decrease in basal, ATP-linked, maximal and reserve OCR in HCC515 and H2122 cell lines (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR measurements in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Reduction of COX6B2 protein using shRNA pools leads to a decrease in reserve OCR in HCC515 and H2122 cell lines.
source: Reduction of COX6B2 protein using shRNA pools (four independent sequences) or siRNA pools (two independent sequences), led to a decrease in basal, ATP-linked, maximal and reserve OCR in HCC515 and H2122 cell lines (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR measurements in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Reduction of COX6B2 protein using siRNA pools leads to a decrease in basal, ATP-linked, maximal and reserve OCR in HCC515 and H2122 cell lines.
source: Reduction of COX6B2 protein using shRNA pools (four independent sequences) or siRNA pools (two independent sequences), led to a decrease in basal, ATP-linked, maximal and reserve OCR in HCC515 and H2122 cell lines (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR measurements in Figure 5B.

claim: sgCOX6B2 cells exhibit attenuated OCR.
source: In agreement with the si and shCOX6B2 data, sgCOX6B2 cells also exhibit attenuated OCR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR measurements in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The reduction in OCR following COX6B2 depletion is accompanied by a reduction in the NAD+/NADH ratio.
source: The reduction in OCR following COX6B2 depletion is accompanied by a reduction in the NAD+/NADH ratio (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by NAD+/NADH measurements in Figure 5C.

claim: Total cellular ATP is decreased following siRNA-mediated COX6B2 depletion across a panel of COX6B2-expressing LUAD cell lines.
source: In addition, total cellular ATP is decreased following siRNA-mediated COX6B2 depletion with two independent siRNA sequences across a panel of COX6B2-expressing LUAD cell lines (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by ATP content measurements in Figure 5D.

claim: Depletion of COX6B2 results in decreased mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Consistent with a loss of electron transport chain function, depletion of COX6B2 resulted in decreased mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 5E) and increased intracellular hydrogen peroxide (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by JC-1 staining data in Figure 5E.

claim: Depletion of COX6B2 results in increased intracellular hydrogen peroxide.
source: Consistent with a loss of electron transport chain function, depletion of COX6B2 resulted in decreased mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 5E) and increased intracellular hydrogen peroxide (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by CM-H2DCFDA staining data in Figure 5F.

claim: COX6B2 is essential for respiration in tumor cells.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that COX6B2 is essential for respiration and mitochondrial integrity in tumor cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on OCR measurements (Figure 5A-B) and other metabolic parameters following COX6B2 depletion.

claim: COX6B2 is essential for mitochondrial integrity in tumor cells.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that COX6B2 is essential for respiration and mitochondrial integrity in tumor cells.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on mitochondrial membrane potential measurements (Figure 5E) and ROS production (Figure 5F) following COX6B2 depletion.

claim: Depletion of COX6B2 for nine days results in a decrease in EdU incorporation.
source: Depletion of COX6B2 for nine days, results in a decrease in EdU incorporation (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation assay data in Figure 6A.

claim: COX6B2-depleted cells are severely compromised in their ability to grow in the absence of an extracellular matrix.
source: Furthermore, these cells are severely compromised in their ability to grow in the absence of an extracellular matrix (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by soft agar assay data in Figure 6B showing reduced colony formation.

claim: Both EdU incorporation and soft agar phenotypes following COX6B2 depletion were recapitulated in sgCOX6B2 cells.
source: Both of these phenotypes were recapitulated in sgCOX6B2 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: siRNA-mediated depletion of COX6B2 enhances cleavage of caspase 3/7.
source: In our original screen, we found that siRNA-mediated depletion of COX6B2 enhances cleavage of caspase 3/7, a phenotype that is rescued in COX6B2-V5 overexpressing cells (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C; Maxfield et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maxfield et al., 2015 and data in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The caspase 3/7 cleavage phenotype following COX6B2 depletion is rescued in COX6B2-V5 overexpressing cells.
source: In our original screen, we found that siRNA-mediated depletion of COX6B2 enhances cleavage of caspase 3/7, a phenotype that is rescued in COX6B2-V5 overexpressing cells (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C; Maxfield et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C showing reduced caspase activity in COX6B2-V5 cells.

claim: Depletion of COX6B2 using a pool of shRNAs results in cleavage of caspase-3 and PARP.
source: In cells where COX6B2 is depleted using a pool of shRNAs, with sequences independent of the those in the siRNA pool, we observed cleavage of caspase-3 and PARP (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6C showing cleaved caspase-3 and PARP.

claim: Cell death markers are induced in sgCOX6B2 cells.
source: These cell death markers are also induced in sgCOX6B2 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The induction of cell death proteins following COX6B2 depletion is accompanied by an increase in Annexin-V staining.
source: The induction of cell death proteins is accompanied by an increase in Annexin-V staining, demonstrating activation of caspase-dependent programmed cell death (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by Annexin-V flow cytometry data in Figure 6D.

claim: COX6B2-depleted cells show an increase in β-galactosidase, suggesting induction of a cellular senescence program.
source: Staining of these cells revealed an increase in β-galactosidase, suggesting induction of a cellular senescence program (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by β-galactosidase staining data in Figure 6F.

claim: Supplementing COX6B2-depleted cells with pyruvate and uridine is insufficient to rescue the viability defects.
source: Supplementing depleted cells with pyruvate and uridine as metabolic and nucleotide fuel was insufficient to rescue the viability defects (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation and senescence data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-F showing no rescue with pyruvate and uridine.

claim: Exposing COX6B2-depleted cells to N-acetyl-l-cysteine (NAC) reduces the extent of cleaved caspase-3 and PARP.
source: However, exposing cells to the ROS scavenger N-acetyl-l-cysteine (NAC) reduced the extent of the cleaved caspase-3 and PARP and β-galactosidase staining (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 6G showing reduced cleaved caspase-3 and PARP with NAC treatment.

claim: Exposing COX6B2-depleted cells to N-acetyl-l-cysteine (NAC) reduces β-galactosidase staining.
source: However, exposing cells to the ROS scavenger N-acetyl-l-cysteine (NAC) reduced the extent of the cleaved caspase-3 and PARP and β-galactosidase staining (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: Supported by β-galactosidase staining data in Figure 6H showing reduced staining with NAC treatment.

claim: COX6B2 suppression reduces ATP, compromises mitochondrial integrity thereby generating excess ROS that leads to apoptosis or senescence.
source: Thus, COX6B2 is essential for survival of LUAD tumor cells as its suppression reduces ATP, compromises mitochondrial integrity thereby generating excess ROS that leads to apoptosis or senescence.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on multiple observations including reduced ATP (Figure 5D), loss of mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 5E), increased ROS (Figure 5F), and induction of apoptosis/senescence markers (Figure 6).

claim: COX6B2-V5 expressing tumors exhibit a 4X greater mass than control after 38 days.
source: After 38 days, COX6B2-V5 tumors exhibit a 4X greater mass than control (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by xenograft tumor mass measurements in Figure 7B.

claim: Depletion of COX6B2 severely reduces tumor growth in vivo.
source: Complementing the gain-of-function phenotype observed, we found that depletion of COX6B2 severely reduces tumor growth and final tumor mass (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: Supported by xenograft tumor volume and mass measurements in Figure 7C-D.

claim: Depletion of COX6B2 severely reduces final tumor mass in vivo.
source: Complementing the gain-of-function phenotype observed, we found that depletion of COX6B2 severely reduces tumor growth and final tumor mass (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: Supported by xenograft tumor mass measurements in Figure 7D.

claim: The anomalous expression of COX6B2 is both necessary and sufficient for growth of LUAD tumors.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that the anomalous expression of COX6B2 is both necessary and sufficient for growth of LUAD tumors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on xenograft data showing both gain-of-function (Figure 7A-B) and loss-of-function (Figure 7C-D) phenotypes.

claim: COX6B2 function appears to differ from COX6B1.
source: Our data indicate that COX6B2 enhances complex IV activity leading to an increase in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. The function of COX6B2 appears to differ from COX6B1, which did not enhance OXPHOS when overexpressed, a finding consistent with previous biochemical analyses that indicate removal of COX6B1 enhances complex IV activity (Weishaupt and Kadenbach, 1992).
evidence: Supported by comparison of OCR data for COX6B2-V5 (Figure 2D,F) versus COX6B1-V5 (Figure 2K) and citation to Weishaupt and Kadenbach, 1992.

claim: COX6B1 (and perhaps B2) are essential for assembly and regulation of complex IV.
source: Based on this cumulative data, we hypothesize that COX6B1 (and perhaps B2) are essential for assembly and regulation of complex IV.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on genetic studies showing mutations in COX6B1 reduce complex IV assembly.

claim: In normal tissues, COX6B1 may regulate complex IV to prevent the generation of excessive and unused energy and damaging ROS.
source: In normal tissues, COX6B1 may regulate complex IV to prevent the generation of excessive and unused energy and also damaging ROS.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about COX6B1 function in normal tissues.

claim: In sperm, COX6B2 expression could promote complex IV dimerization and incorporation into supercomplexes to promote efficient OXPHOS and limit ROS production.
source: In sperm, where ATP demand is high, COX6B2 expression could promote complex IV dimerization and incorporation into supercomplexes to promote efficient OXPHOS and limit ROS production that would otherwise damage DNA (Agarwal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about COX6B2 function in sperm, supported by citation to Agarwal et al., 2014 regarding ROS damage to sperm DNA.

claim: COX6B2 function may be particularly important during early tumorigenesis, where a highly hypoxic environment can lead to proliferative arrest and excessive ROS generation.
source: This function may be particularly important during early tumorigenesis, where a highly hypoxic environment can lead to proliferative arrest and excessive ROS generation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the role of COX6B2 in early tumorigenesis.

claim: Tumor cells that express and engage the COX6B2-based, sperm-specific mechanism can overcome an innate barrier to transformation that would otherwise restrict cell survival.
source: We propose that tumor cells that express and engage the COX6B2-based, sperm-specific mechanism can overcome this innate barrier to transformation that would otherwise restrict cell survival.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about how COX6B2 contributes to tumorigenesis.

claim: The loss of COX6B2 would be expected to reduce ATP levels and the NAD+/NADH ratio and slow proliferation, but not necessarily kill tumor cells.
source: As COX6B2 enhances OXPHOS, its loss would be expected to reduce ATP levels and the NAD+/NADH ratio and slow proliferation, but not necessarily kill tumor cells.
evidence: This is a logical inference about expected consequences of COX6B2 loss.

claim: Tumor cell glycolytic pathways should theoretically compensate for reduced energy generation following COX6B2 loss.
source: Tumor cell glycolytic pathways should theoretically compensate for reduced energy generation.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on knowledge of tumor metabolism.

claim: The presence of COX6B1 should be able to support complex IV function in the absence of COX6B2.
source: Moreover, the presence of COX6B1 should be able to support complex IV function.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on COX6B1 being the somatic isoform of COX6B2.

claim: COX6B2-depleted cells are highly dependent upon OXPHOS for survival.
source: This finding implies that these cells are highly dependent upon OXPHOS for survival.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that COX6B2 depletion leads to cell death despite the presence of COX6B1.

claim: The loss of COX6B2 may promote apoptosis due to a collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential and cytochrome c egress.
source: In addition, the loss of COX6B2 may promote apoptosis due to a collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential and cytochrome c egress (Smaili et al., 2001; Tai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations to Smaili et al., 2001 and Tai et al., 2017.

claim: OXPHOS contributes to >80% of total ATP production in tumor cells.
source: First, OXPHOS contributes to >80% of total ATP production in tumor cells, which is essential for satisfying the demands of proliferation and tumor progression (Rao et al., 2019; Lissanu Deribe et al., 2018; Zu and Guppy, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rao et al., 2019; Lissanu Deribe et al., 2018; Zu and Guppy, 2004.

claim: OXPHOS provides electron acceptors to generate metabolic intermediates (e.g. aspartate) that are required for continued cell division.
source: Second, OXPHOS provides electron acceptors to generate metabolic intermediates (e.g. aspartate) that are required for continued cell division (Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sullivan et al., 2015.

claim: Tumor cells exhibit enhanced sensitivity to inhibitors of OXPHOS.
source: Third, tumor cells exhibit enhanced sensitivity to inhibitors of OXPHOS (Nayak et al., 2018; Scotland et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nayak et al., 2018 and Scotland et al., 2013.

claim: Isoform switching of complex IV subunits is observed in tumors and is associated with aggressive malignant behaviors.
source: Fourth, isoform switching of complex IV subunits is observed in tumors and is associated with aggressive malignant behaviors (Oliva et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Minton et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Oliva et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016; Minton et al., 2016.

claim: OXPHOS is upregulated and essential for survival during ER-stress, hypoxia and glucose limiting conditions, and exposure to targeted therapies.
source: Finally, OXPHOS is upregulated and essential for survival during ER-stress, hypoxia and glucose limiting conditions, and exposure to targeted therapies (Balsa et al., 2019; Ikeda et al., 2019; Fukuda et al., 2007; Guièze et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Balsa et al., 2019; Ikeda et al., 2019; Fukuda et al., 2007; Guièze et al., 2019.

claim: Inhibition of OXPHOS is a tractable therapeutic entry point for treating cancer.
source: Based on these and a vast array of additional data, it is accepted that inhibition of OXPHOS is a tractable therapeutic entry point for treating cancer (Weinberg and Chandel, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weinberg and Chandel, 2015 and general scientific consensus.

claim: Metformin has demonstrated anti-proliferative activities and reduction of tumor incidence through the inhibition of Complex I.
source: Indeed, extensive studies with metformin have demonstrated anti-proliferative activities and reduction of tumor incidence through the inhibition of Complex I (Weinberg and Chandel, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weinberg and Chandel, 2015.

claim: ETC inhibitors like metformin cannot discriminate between tumor or normal cells, limiting their therapeutic window.
source: However, this and other ETC inhibitors cannot discriminate between tumor or normal cells, limiting their therapeutic window.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the limitations of current ETC inhibitors.

claim: Enhanced accumulation of COX6B2 is an acquired trait that is essential for OXPHOS in LUAD and perhaps additional cancers.
source: We propose that enhanced accumulation of COX6B2 is an acquired trait that is essential for OXPHOS in LUAD and perhaps additional cancers.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the data showing COX6B2 expression in LUAD tumors and its role in enhancing OXPHOS.

claim: Elevated COX6B2 protein expression is a functional enrollment biomarker for OXPHOS-inhibitor-based treatment.
source: At minimum, elevated COX6B2 protein expression is a functional enrollment biomarker for OXPHOS-inhibitor-based treatment.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the finding that COX6B2 is essential for OXPHOS in LUAD.

claim: COX6B2 structural elements that are distinct from COX6B1 could represent targets for small molecule inhibitors.
source: Moreover, COX6B2 structural elements that are distinct from COX6B1 could represent targets for small molecule inhibitors.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about potential therapeutic targeting of COX6B2.

claim: COX6B2 represents an ideal candidate for immunotherapy because it has a bona fide tumorigenic function.
source: We propose that COX6B2 represents an ideal candidate for immunotherapy because it has a bona fide tumorigenic function.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the demonstrated tumorigenic function of COX6B2 and its classification as a CTA.

claim: Sequence differences between COX6B2 and COX6B1 could permit antigen recognition by patient immune cells and act as targets of adoptive T-cell transfer.
source: Specifically, sequence differences between COX6B2 and COX6B1 could permit antigen recognition by patient immune cells and thus act as targets of adoptive T-cell transfer.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about potential immunotherapy targeting of COX6B2.

claim: Cancer testis antigens (CTAs) are proteins whose expression is normally restricted to the testis but anomalously activated in human cancer.
source: Cancer testis antigens (CTAs) are proteins whose expression is normally restricted to the testis but anomalously activated in human cancer.
evidence: This is the definition of cancer testis antigens, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: In sperm, a number of CTAs support energy generation.
source: In sperm, a number of CTAs support energy generation, however, whether they contribute to tumor metabolism is not understood.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CTA function in sperm.

claim: Whether CTAs contribute to tumor metabolism is not understood.
source: In sperm, a number of CTAs support energy generation, however, whether they contribute to tumor metabolism is not understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of writing.

claim: The findings reveal a previously unappreciated, tumor-specific metabolic pathway hijacked from sperm motility.
source: Our findings reveal a previously unappreciated, tumor-specific metabolic pathway hijacked from one of the most ATP-intensive processes in the animal kingdom: sperm motility.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the overall findings of the study.

claim: Tumors frequently activate genes whose expression is otherwise restricted to testis.
source: Tumors frequently activate genes whose expression is otherwise restricted to testis; these genes are known collectively as cancer-testis antigens (CT-antigens, CTAs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer testis antigens.

claim: The expression of CTAs outside their native and immune privileged site has been the basis for immunotherapeutic approaches including vaccines and adoptive T-cell therapy.
source: The expression of these genes outside their native and immune privileged site has been the basis for immunotherapeutic approaches including vaccines and adoptive T-cell therapy (Hunder et al., 2008; Gjerstorff et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hunder et al., 2008 and Gjerstorff et al., 2015.

claim: Functional knowledge of the contribution of CTAs to neoplastic behaviors has significantly lagged behind immune-targeting.
source: Historically, functional knowledge of the contribution of these proteins, if any, to neoplastic behaviors has significantly lagged behind immune-targeting.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical state of CTA research.

claim: CTAs have been implicated in tumor cell survival, TGF-β signaling, mitotic fidelity, polyadenylation, mRNA export, tumor suppressor silencing, and DNA damage repair.
source: In recent years, the functional characterization of CTAs has gained broader interest and these proteins have been implicated in tumor cell survival, TGF-β signaling, mitotic fidelity, polyadenylation, mRNA export, tumor suppressor silencing, and DNA damage repair (Gibbs and Whitehurst, 2018; Viphakone et al., 2015; Nichols et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gibbs and Whitehurst, 2018; Viphakone et al., 2015; Nichols et al., 2018.

claim: Multiple reports indicate that anomalous expression of testis proteins can be engaged to support the tumorigenic program.
source: Multiple reports now indicate that anomalous expression of testis proteins can be engaged to support the tumorigenic program.
evidence: This is a summary of recent findings in the field.

claim: The biased expression pattern of CTAs to tumors and testis may offer an extraordinarily broad therapeutic window if they can be targeted directly.
source: The biased expression pattern of these proteins to tumors and testis may offer an extraordinarily broad therapeutic window if they can be targeted directly.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about the therapeutic potential of targeting CTAs.

claim: Mammalian sperm have a tremendous energy demand required for motility while preserving the integrity of their DNA cargo within the hostile environment of the female reproductive tract.
source: One unique aspect of mammalian sperm physiology is the tremendous energy demand required for motility while preserving the integrity of their precious DNA cargo within the hostile environment of the female reproductive tract.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sperm physiology.

claim: Sperm contain a number of tissue-specific protein isoforms for glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) that mediate the increase in ATP production.
source: To meet this demand, sperm contain a number of tissue-specific protein isoforms for glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) that mediate the increase in ATP production.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sperm metabolism.

claim: Lactate dehydrogenase C (LDHC) is a testis-specific isoform of the terminal enzyme in glycolysis that catalyzes the reduction of pyruvate to lactate essential for male fertility.
source: For example, lactate dehydrogenase C, LDHC, is a testis-specific isoform of the terminal enzyme in glycolysis that catalyzes the reduction of pyruvate to lactate essential for male fertility (Odet et al., 2008; Krisfalusi et al., 2006; Li et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Odet et al., 2008; Krisfalusi et al., 2006; Li et al., 1989.

claim: mRNA encoding LDHC is undetectable in normal tissue.
source: mRNA encoding of either LDHC or COX6B2 is undetectable in normal tissue, but both are upregulated in a number of different tumor derived cell lines, classifying them as CTAs (Maxfield et al., 2015, (CTpedia (http://www.cta.lncc.br/index.php))).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maxfield et al., 2015 and CTpedia database.

claim: LDHC is upregulated in tumor derived cell lines.
source: mRNA encoding of either LDHC or COX6B2 is undetectable in normal tissue, but both are upregulated in a number of different tumor derived cell lines, classifying them as CTAs (Maxfield et al., 2015, (CTpedia (http://www.cta.lncc.br/index.php))).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maxfield et al., 2015 and CTpedia database.

claim: It is unclear whether LDHC and COX6B2 support metabolic programs in tumor cells.
source: However, it is unclear whether these proteins support metabolic programs in tumor cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge at the time of writing, which the study aims to address.

claim: Depletion of COX6B2 activates cleaved caspase 3/7 in cell lines derived from breast, melanoma and NSCLC.
source: Using a large-scale functional genomics approaches, we previously found that depletion of COX6B2 activates cleaved caspase 3/7 in cell lines derived from breast, melanoma and NSCLC, with the most potent activation in H1299 NSCLC cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Maxfield et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maxfield et al., 2015 and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The most potent activation of cleaved caspase 3/7 by COX6B2 depletion occurs in H1299 NSCLC cells.
source: Using a large-scale functional genomics approaches, we previously found that depletion of COX6B2 activates cleaved caspase 3/7 in cell lines derived from breast, melanoma and NSCLC, with the most potent activation in H1299 NSCLC cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Maxfield et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maxfield et al., 2015 and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Tumors engrafted subcutaneously encounter a highly hypoxic environment (~0.08–0.8% O2).
source: Importantly, tumors engrafted subcutaneously encounter a highly hypoxic environment (~0.08–0.8% O2) (Helmlinger et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Helmlinger et al., 1997.

claim: Supercomplexes are hypothesized to promote local channeling of substrates, trapping of reactive intermediates and/or subunit stabilization.
source: Supercomplexes contain multiple electron transport sub-complexes containing complex III and IV and are hypothesized to promote local channeling of substrates, trapping of reactive intermediates and/or subunit stabilization (Acín-Pérez et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Acín-Pérez et al., 2008.

claim: Supercomplexes are hypothesized to enhance electron transport activity without a compensatory increase in ROS.
source: Supercomplexes are hypothesized to enhance electron transport activity without a compensatory increase in ROS (Maranzana et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maranzana et al., 2013.

claim: Mitochondrial OXPHOS has been linked to proliferation via regulation of the NAD+/NADH ratio.
source: Mitochondrial OXPHOS has been linked to proliferation via regulation of the NAD+/NADH ratio, which is elevated in COX6B2-V5 overexpressing cells (Figure 2H; Birsoy et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Birsoy et al., 2015 and Sullivan et al., 2015.

claim: Tissue-specific complex IV isoforms may promote supercomplex formation and selectively increase ATP production in tumor cells.
source: Recently, a number of reports have suggested that tissue-specific complex IV isoforms may promote supercomplex formation and selectively and specifically increase ATP production in tumor cells (Maranzana et al., 2013; Ikeda et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maranzana et al., 2013 and Ikeda et al., 2019.

claim: Isoforms of complex IV subunits can be selectively expressed to permit adaptation to tissue-specific needs or environmental conditions.
source: Isoforms of complex IV subunits can be selectively expressed to permit adaptation to tissue-specific needs or environmental conditions (Sinkler et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sinkler et al., 2017.

claim: Hypoxia is reported to regulate complex IV subunit expression and permit continued respiration in low oxygen.
source: In particular, hypoxia is reported to regulate complex IV subunit expression and permit continued respiration in low oxygen (Ikeda et al., 2019; Hayashi et al., 2015; Fukuda et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ikeda et al., 2019; Hayashi et al., 2015; Fukuda et al., 2007.
